## Abstract

Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors have achieved positive responses in myeloproliferative neoplasms, but at the expense of decreased natural killer (NK) cell numbers and compromised function. Selective JAK2 inhibition may also have a role in preventing and treating graft-vs-host disease after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Although JAK inhibitors can impair monocyte-derived dendritic cell (moDC) activation and function and suppress effector T-cell responses, the effects on NK cells and the relevant mechanisms remain undefined. Using common γ_{c} cytokines and distinct human dendritic cell (DC) subtypes, we compared the effects of a JAK2-specific (TG101348) with a less selective JAK1/2 (ruxolitinib) inhibitor on NK-cell activation and function. Ruxolitinib treatment completely blocked IL2, IL15, and DC-mediated STAT5 phosphorylation, along with the capacity of NK cells to secrete IFNγ or lyse NK cell– sensitive targets. Only NK-cell proliferation stimulated by monocyte-derived DCs (moDCs) resisted ruxolitinib treatment. In contrast, TG101348 treatment of stimulated NK cells resulted in far less functional compromise. TG101348 completely inhibited only soluble IL15-mediated STAT5 phosphorylation, which Langerhans-type DCs (LCs), presenting membrane-bound IL15 in trans, could salvage. These results demonstrate that ruxolitinib's nonselective inhibition of JAK1/2 results in profound NK-cell dysfunction by blocking downstream pSTAT5,hence providing a persuasive rationale for the development of selective JAK2 inhibitors for immunotherapeutic applications.

## Introduction

Patients with hematologic and lymphoid malignancies can benefit greatly from allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (alloHSCT), achieving long-term cures in many cases but too often at the expense of graft-vs-host disease (GvHD). A major goal in limiting complications after alloHSCT therefore involves targeting key pro-inflammatory mediators, like IL6, IL23, and IFNγ that can promote graft-vs-host disease (GvHD)(1), without broadly impairing the immune response that mediates the desired graft-vs-leukemia or graft-vs-tumor (GvL/GvT) effect. We previously found that a targeted JAK2 inhibitor (TG101348)(2)facilitated induction of strong and durable tolerance by T cells to specific alloantigens, without disrupting protective responses to third party antigens(3). Expansion of Th1 and Th17 cells also decreased(3). These interactions in vitro corresponded, respectively, to prevention of GvHD and maintenance of effective immunity against pathogenic and tumor antigens in vivo, thus validating specific JAK2 inhibition as a potential treatment for GvHD.

The JAK proteins, which are the principle gatekeepers for cytokine signaling, comprise four nonreceptor tyrosine kinases that include JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, and TYK2(4). Activation of these JAK proteins results in the downstream phosphorylation of one or more STAT proteins, which in turn function as transcription factors for genes involved in cell differentiation and growth(4). Our initial work focused on moDC-stimulated T-cell responses and the JAK2-specific inhibitor,TG101348 (fedratinib), studied in vitro because of its ability to target IL6, IL23, and IFNγ. The development of Wernicke's, led to withdrawal of this particular drug from further development encephalopathy in 1.4% of the patients on a phase 3 clinical trial, however (5). In addition to T cells, NK cells also play a key role in promoting stem cell engraftment and mediating the desired GvL/GvT effect(6-8). Because of the potential utility of other drugs in development for specifically inhibiting JAK2 to treat GvHD, contrasted with the increasing use of nonselective JAK1/2 inhibition as salvage treatment for corticosteroid-refractory GvHD(9), it is critical to understand whether, and how, selective vs nonselective JAK inhibition may affect NK cells.

Ruxolitinib, received Breakthrough Therapy Designation in 2016, from the US Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of acute GvHD. In contrast to the selective ability of TG101348 to inhibit JAK2(2),however, ruxolitinib inhibits both JAK1 and JAK2 equally well(10). This activity may impair NK-cell function insofar as IL2 and IL15, key cytokines that activate NK cells and maintain their homeostasis(11),use JAK1 (and JAK3) to mediate STAT5 phosphorylation(12). Reports of opportunistic infections in the setting of ruxolitinib treatment are consistent with functionally impaired NK cells, or even antigen-presenting cells, contributing to these complications(13-15). In fact, ruxolitinib does impair the migration and function of murine DCs in vivo, as well as the differentiation, maturation, and activation of human moDCs in vitro(13). Apropos of these findings, moDCs are the specific human DC subtype with stimulatory capacity for NK cells, through their secretion of large amounts of IL12p70(16,17). We have therefore focused on NK cells and investigated whether ruxolitinib treatment negatively affects NK-cell proliferation and function in vitro, comparing its effects with selective JAK2 inhibition and distinguishing soluble cytokine activation of NK cells from that stimulated by DCs. It is important to define these parameters in view of the potential consequences of using ruxolitinib in the management of GvHD after alloHSCT.

## Materials and Methods

### Primary human cells

NK cells were isolated from healthy donor leukocyte concentrates (Greater New York Blood Center, American Red Cross) or myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN)patient blood samples (Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC) Hematologic Oncology Tissue Bank) by negative selection as previously described(17). All collection and use of human specimens adhered to protocols reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review and Privacy Board of MSKCC.

### Media & cell lines

Primary human cell cultures used complete RPMI-1640 medium (MSKCC Media Prep Core Facility) with 10 mM HEPES, 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Media Laboratory, MSKCC), 50 μM2-ME (GibcoBRL Life Technologies), 1% L-glutamine(GibcoBRL), and heat-inactivated, pooled human serum (10% v/v; Gemini Bio-Products). All media and reagents were endotoxin-free based on negative result from manufacturer or Limulus Amebocyte Lysate Kit (Cambrex) tested in-house.

The MHC class-I^{−} cell line, K562, derived from human erythroleukemia (original source, Dr. 
### JAK Inhibitors

The JAK inhibitors TG101348 (inhibitor of JAK2) and ruxolitinib (inhibits JAK1/2) were synthesized by the MSKCC Organic Synthesis Core Facility. TG101348 (3) and ruxolitinib were used at the optimal working concentration of 1μM, as determined by an EC_{50} dose response curve (Supplementary Fig. S1A) and previously published reports (15, 18). JAK2 suppressive activity was confirmed by measuring IL6-induced STAT3 phosphorylation among TG101348 or ruxolitinib treated T cells (Supplementary Fig.S1B).

### Generation & maturation of dendritic cells

Langerhans-type DCs (LCs) and monocyte derived DCs (moDCs) were generated exactly as published(19,20). Immature moDCs or LCs were terminally matured and activated with TLR3 ligand poly(I:C) (25 μg/mL, Invivogen) (17) or inflammatory cytokines(19), respectively. Poly(I:C) induces the highest amount of IL12p70 production by moDCs, whereas LCs produce little to no IL12p70 regardless of stimulus(17). In contrast, the combination of IL1, IL6, TNFα, and PGE_{2} is the most effective stimulus for IL15 production by LCs; and moDCs produce little to no IL15 under any condition(19,20). Hereafter, we refer to these matured cultured cell types separately as moDC_{poly}orLC_{cyto}, or in the aggregate as DCs.

### DC-NK coculture

Purified NK cells were stimulated with moDC_{poly} or LC_{cyto} at a ratio of 10:1 (NK: moDC) for six days(17). 1μMTG101348, 1μMruxolitinib, or 0.01% DMSO vehicle control was added once at the start of DC-NK cocultures.


1 × 10^{5} freshly isolated bulk NK cells were cultured either alone, or with 200 IU/mL recombinant human IL2 (Chiron), 10 ng/mL recombinant human IL15 (CellGenix), or moDC_{poly} for 6 d. TG101348, ruxolitinib, or DMSO control was added once on day 0. NK-cell proliferation was determined by a colorimetric assay according to the manufacturer's instructions (CellTiter 96 AQ_{ueous} One Solution Cell Proliferation Assay; Promega). Metabolically active cells reduce a tetrazolium compound, which is added for the final 4 h of the coculture, into a colored formazan product that is detected at 490nm.

### Phosphorylation of STAT proteins

STAT5 signaling: PBMCs (1 × 10^{6} cells /mL) were stimulated overnight with IL15 (7.5 ng/mL; CellGenix)(21), harvested, then serum-starved for 1hr in the presence of TG101348, ruxolitinib, or DMSO control. The cells were then pulsed with IL2 (EC_{50} 50 IU/mL; Chiron), IL15 (EC_{50} 2.7 ng/mL; CellGenix), allogeneic moDCs or LCs (1:1 ratio) for 15 minutes followed by fixation (CytoFix; BD Biosciences)and permeabilization. Cells were stained for CD3 (Clone UCHT1) and CD56 to identify NK cells (CD3^{−}CD56^{+}) and intracellular Alexa Fluor 647 anti-STAT5 (pY694; BD Biosciences). Where indicated, IL15Rα was blocked on both moDCs and LCs with anti-IL15Rα(5μg/mL)or IgG control (R&D Systems).

STAT4 signaling: PBMCs (1 × 10^{6} cells /mL) were stimulated for 2 d with 100 IU/mL IL2 (Chiron) to facilitate optimal IL12R induction(22). Cells were harvested and serum-starved for 1 hour in the presence of TG101348, ruxolitinib, or DMSO. Cells were then pulsed with allogeneic moDCs or LCs (1:1 ratio), matured moDC or LC supernatant, or 100 IU/mL IL12p70 (R&D Systems) for 90 min (23). pSTAT4 expression was ascertained using an intracellular PE- or Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated anti-STAT4 (pY693; BD Biosceinces).

STAT3 signaling: This was assessed in JAK inhibitor-treated T cells as published(3).

### Chromium release assay

NK-cellcytolytic activity was assessed in standard ^{51}Cr release assays(20) against K562 targets, where one of the JAK inhibitors or DMSO was added once on day 0 of the 6-d coculture. The percentage of specific cytotoxicity was calculated using the formula 100 × (cpm experimental − cpm spontaneous)/(cpm maximum – cpm spontaneous).

## Results

### Nonselective JAK1/2 inhibition reduced NK-cell numbers and function among treated MPN patients

In accordance with published data(14, 15), ruxolitinib is detrimental to NK-cell function in vivo. Ruxolitinib significantly decreased the number of circulating NK cells in patients treated for MPN (Supplementary Fig. S2A). NK cells from patients receiving ruxolitinib had impaired lytic activity, manifested by defective degranulation (reduced CD107a), and diminished IFNγ release against K562 cell targets (Supplementary Fig. S2B). These data corroborate ruxolitinib'ssuppression of NK-cell numbers and function in patients treated for MPN.

### MoDC_{poly}-stimulated NK-cell receptor repertoire is not affected by JAK inhibition

Bulk NK cells cocultured for six days with moDC_{poly} in the presence of TG101348, ruxolitinib, or DMSO diluent control underwent extensive phenotyping of both activating and inhibitory NK-cell receptor expression. Compared with DMSO control, neither of the JAK inhibitors altered NK-cell expression of CD56, CD16, CD94, KIRs, LIR1, NKG2A, CD57, NKG2D, CD161, NKp30, NKp44, or NKp46 (cite37†Fig. 2A ). The selective JAK2 inhibitor, TG101348, also impaired NK-cell proliferative responses to soluble IL2 or IL15, but not as completely as did ruxolitinib. Allogeneic moDCs, matured with poly I:C to maximize IL12p70 secretion(17), overcame the suppressive effects of both ruxolitinib and TG101348on NK-cell proliferation.

Nonselective JAK1/2 inhibition by ruxolitinib significantly reduced expression of the early activation marker, CD69, by NK cells pulsed with soluble IL2 or IL15 (Fig. 2B, left). Stimulation by allogeneic moDC_{poly} secreting abundant IL12p70 largely restored CD69 expression. In contrast, selective JAK2 inhibition by TG101348 minimally reduced CD69 on NK cells; and hence there was no significant reversal by moDC_{poly} (Fig. 2B, right).

Some lytic activity was retained by the TG101348 (P =0.071 relative to the DMSO vehicle control) but not by the ruxolitinib condition. *P =0.01-0.05; **P =0.001-0.01; ***P ≤ 0.001;ns=not significant.

### Effects of different JAK inhibitors and DC subtypes on STAT5 signaling in NK cells

MoDC_{poly} can directly prime NK cells by providing abundant IL12p70, which LC_{cyto} do not secrete(16,17). Conversely, moDC_{poly} produce substantially less IL15 than LC_{cyto}, which express an abundance of the membrane-associated IL15Rα/IL15 complex (20) and support activated NK-cell viability and homeostasis but cannot activate resting NK cells(16). IL12p70and the common γ_{c} cytokines, e.g., IL2 and IL15, can independently induce STAT4 and STAT5 phosphorylation in NK cells (21,23).

To understand how JAK1/2 versus JAK2 blockade differentially affects NK-cell STAT5 activation, we exposed NK cells to IL2, IL15, moDC_{poly}, or LC_{cyto} stimuli in the presence of ruxolitinib or TG101348. One representative experiment of three is shown with the bar graph depicting pooled data (mean ± SD) normalized to vehicle control. *P =0.01-0.05; **P =0.001-0.01; ***P ≤ 0.001; ****P ≤ 0.0001; ns=not significant.

IL12p70 binding to its heterodimeric receptor provides binding sites for Tyk2 and JAK2, which in turn phosphorylate STAT4, leading to IFNγ secretion by NK cells(27). In accordance with copious IL12p70 secretion by moDC_{poly}(17), both the cells and the moDC_{poly} supernatant mediated STAT4 phosphorylation, which was significantly reduced by exposure to either TG101348 or ruxolitinib (Fig. 5A). The ability of moDC_{poly} supernatant to induce pSTAT4 was solely due to secreted factors, because the cytokines used to maturemoDCs [poly(I:C), IL4, and GM-CSF] were unable to elicit any STAT4 phosphorylation (data not shown). LC_{cyto} or their supernatants were equally inactive in phosphorylating STAT4, owing to their lack of IL12p70(16,17).

### JAK2, not JAK1/2, inhibition preserves NK-cell STAT5 over STAT4 phosphorylation

Predominance of pSTAT5 over pSTAT4 promotes human NK-cell proliferation, lytic function, and memory-like differentiation(28,29). moDC_{poly}-stimulated NK cells exposed to DMSO vehicle control achieved a pSTAT5:pSTAT4 ratio of 2.4:1 (Fig. 5B and C). Phosphorylation of both STAT4 and STAT5 was partially reduced by TG101348, though the pSTAT5:pSTAT4 ratio was maintained. Ruxolitinib, however, almost completely eliminated both pSTAT4 and pSTAT5, again underscoring the more profound effects that it exerts on NK-cell-based immune function (Fig. 5B and C).

## Discussion

Nonselective JAK1/2 inhibition impairs cytokine-mediated NK-cell activation and function in patients treated with ruxolitinib, and we have defined several of the key mechanisms. Our findings clarify why individuals receiving ruxolitinib are at increased risk of acquiring opportunistic infections(13-15). These include significant cytomegalovirus reactivation in patients given salvage treatment with ruxolitinib for steroid-refractory GvHD, although the incidence is not necessarily worse than added treatment with other immune suppressants and, in any case, difficult to distinguish from the contribution of steroids(30).

The immune suppressive effect of pan-JAK or JAK1/2 inhibition is broad, blunting T-cell as well as NK-cell responses reported here. Although others have described defects in human NK-cell function mediated by ruxolitinib, we provide evidence that selective JAK2 blockade permits greater NK-cell activity than nonselective targeting of both JAK1 and 2. We also show that moDCs attenuate the functional impairment of NK cells mediated by either JAK inhibitor, primarily with regard to proliferation and expression of the activation marker CD69, though much less so with regard to STAT phosphorylation and the development of NK-cell lytic activity and IFNγ secretion. MoDCs provide abundant IL12p70 that can signal through an alternative JAK family member, Tyk-2, and still phosphorylate STAT4(31), which in turn supports IFNγ secretion. LCs restore STAT5 phosphorylation in NK cells exposed to JAK2, but not JAK1/2, blockade; and this depends on the presentation of membrane bound IL15Rα/IL15 on LCs in trans to the responding NK cells. Selective JAK2 inhibition also maintains the physiologic ratio(29)of activated STAT5 to STAT4 among NK cells stimulated by allogeneic moDCs, whereas such signal transduction is abolished when targeting JAK1/2. A predominance of pSTAT5 among activated NK cells is required for their survival, lytic function, and proliferation(28,29).

Human moDCs activated by poly(I:C)mimic the maturation program mediated by viral pathogens. Poly(I:C) significantly increases moDC production of bioactive IL12p70, which promotes NK-cell maturation and activation among otherwise hyporesponsive KIR^{−}NKG2A^{−} precursors(17). Others have shown that expanding memory NK cells, which have the potential to control CMV reactivation(32)and mediate GVL(33), also require IL12p70. Cellular processes induced by IL12p70 act through JAK2- and Tyk2-mediated phosphorylation events to execute proper signal transduction. We confirm that ruxolitinib or TG101348 suppresses JAK2 activation of STAT4 by IL12p70(29). Unlike T cells, NK cells require Tyk2 phosphorylation for their activation and proliferation(31). While both JAK inhibitors display off-target suppression of Tyk2 (TG101348 Tyk2 K_{d}=450nM and ruxolitinib Tyk2 K_{d}= 1400nM, Kinome SCAN, http://lincs.hms.harvard.edu/), stimulation by moDCs_{poly}, which produce copious IL12p70, is sufficient to facilitate NK-cell proliferation.
